strengths: The core idea is simple and well-motivated: the paper provides a Fourier-space analysis (Eq. 11, progression map in Fig. 2b) showing that low-frequency modes converge early during reverse diffusion, and uses this to justify dynamically annealing positional extrapolation (κ(t) = λs·t^λt) so that late denoising steps operate closer to the training PE regime.
The method is genuinely training-free and adds no inference overhead, making it immediately practical on pre-trained DiT models such as FLUX.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: text-to-image on DrawBench and Aesthetic-4K at multiple resolutions and aspect ratios (Table 1), class-conditional ImageNet generation on FiTv2 (Table 3), a human preference study (Table 2), a resolution-scaling analysis up to 6144² (Fig. 5), an ablation over scheduler designs (Tables 5, 6), and a direct comparison to the closest prior art, Lumina-Next Time-Aware Scaled RoPE (Table 4), which DYPE clearly beats under identical conditions.

The gains grow with resolution (e.g., DY-YaRN vs. YaRN at 4096² on DrawBench: CLIP 26.94 vs 25.71, IR 0.15 vs -0.34), which supports the central claim that dynamic PE scheduling matters most in the extreme extrapolation regime.

The paper is honest about the relationship to Lumina-Next, explaining in Appendix B and Fig. 7 why its interpolation direction (toward no-scaling, matching trained PE conditions) differs from prior time-aware RoPE (toward stronger interpolation).
weaknesses: The connection between the spectral analysis and the specific scheduler form is loose. Eq. 11 and the progression map (Fig. 2b) motivate annealing extrapolation over time, but the chosen family κ(t) = λs·t^λt and hyperparameters (λs = λt = 2, plus α, β = 1, 32) are empirically tuned rather than derived from the analysis; no principled prescription is given for choosing them at new resolutions, which weakens reproducibility and the 'principled' framing.

Novelty is incremental. Time-aware RoPE scheduling already exists (Lumina-Next); the contribution is essentially reversing the interpolation direction and tuning when extrapolation should decay. The spectral observation (coarse-to-fine diffusion) is well known (cited: Rissanen et al., Hoogeboom et al., Chen et al.).

Several evaluation concerns: FID values on Aesthetic-4K are very large (~180-200) with unclear setup validity after downsampling; improvements in CLIPScore at some settings are small (e.g., Aesthetic-4K 3072×2048: 29.20 vs 29.12); the resolution-scaling analysis and human study use only 20 prompts with no statistical significance testing; the FreeScale comparison (Table 7) is cross-backbone (SDXL vs FLUX) and not apples-to-apples.

Presentation quality issues undermine polish: the abstract states 'Project page is available at' with no link; the introduction cites 'YourTeam, 2025' with a placeholder bibliography entry (arXiv:2025.xxxxx); Table 1 baseline numbers are inconsistent with the ablation tables' FLUX/NTK/YaRN numbers (different prompt subsets, but this is confusing); typos in Appendix B ('exiting', 'hat low-frequencies').
Only one T2I backbone (FLUX.1-Krea-dev) and one class-conditional model (FiTv2-XL/2) are tested; generality across DiT architectures and RoPE bases is not established.
There is no explicit limitations section discussing failure modes (e.g., degradation at 6144² is mentioned only in passing in Fig. 5) or the sensitivity of results to λs, λt across resolutions.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: the Fourier-space analysis in Sec. 3.1 (Eq. 11-12, Fig. 2) cleanly shows that low-frequency components of the diffused sample converge early while high frequencies evolve throughout, and the method exploits this by annealing the RoPE scaling factor over diffusion time so that the denoiser increasingly operates under its training PE conditions.

The method is genuinely training-free and adds no sampling overhead, and is validated on two model families (FLUX text-to-image and FiTv2 class-conditional ImageNet) across multiple resolutions, aspect ratios, and extreme panoramas, with consistent (if sometimes modest) gains over static PI/NTK/YaRN baselines.

The paper includes useful ablations (Appendix D) over scheduler families, λs/λt values, and where to apply κ(t) in YaRN, plus a comparison to the closest prior work (Time-Aware Scaled RoPE of Lumina-Next, Appendix B, Tab. 4), and a human study and resolution-scaling analysis that probe the method's limits (degradation at 6144²).
weaknesses: Severe citation and manuscript hygiene problems: a literal placeholder reference ('Placeholder YourTeam. Fit v2: Scaling diffusion transformers... arXiv:2025.xxxxx, 2025') remains in the bibliography, the project page URL is empty ('Project page is available at'), FLUX is cited to a GitHub repo under the wrong authorship ('Lee et al., 2025'), and the NTK-aware citation lists arXiv:2306.15595 which is the position-interpolation paper. Such sloppiness undermines trust in the scholarship.

Reported numbers are internally inconsistent: e.g., in Table 5 the 3072² FLUX baseline gives CLIP 25.33 / NTK 25.83 / YaRN 27.32, while Table 1 at the same resolution reports 25.11 / 26.07 / 27.92 with no explanation. The FiTv2 Table 3 also contains implausible values (FiTv2 baseline sFID 38.90 vs. extrapolation methods at 22.63, IS collapsing to 23.10 for PI, recall dropping to 0.16), suggesting evaluation-protocol issues that are not discussed.

Baselines are narrow: the main comparison is only static PI/NTK/YaRN applied to the same model. Recent training-free frequency-based and resolution-extrapolation approaches applicable to DiTs (e.g., FouriScale, HiDiffusion, randomized positional encodings) are discussed in related work but not compared; the single external comparison (FreeScale, SDXL-based) in Appendix E is not a controlled comparison.

The connection between the spectral analysis and the specific scheduler κ(t)=λs·t^λt is heuristic rather than derived; λs=λt=2 are hand-tuned (Appendix C/D), and no analysis connects the fitted progression map γ(f,t) to the chosen functional form, so the 'principled' framing overstates the derivation.

Novelty is incremental relative to Lumina-Next's time-aware RoPE scaling (which the authors acknowledge and argue against): the contribution is essentially applying a different, better-tuned time-dependent scaling schedule to existing LLM extrapolation methods.

FID on Aesthetic-Eval@4096 is computed with only 195 images and yields values in the 146-260 range, which is noisy and of questionable meaning; no variance/significance reporting is given for any quantitative table. The human study (20 prompts, 50 raters, 87-90% preference) reports no statistical testing or rater-selection details.

There is no limitations or ethics discussion section; degradation beyond 6144² is only mentioned in passing in Fig. 5, and the observed portrait/landscape bias and the dependence on hyperparameters at each resolution are not analyzed.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: it connects the well-documented coarse-to-fine spectral progression of the diffusion process to the choice of positional encoding scaling, which is a clean and novel framing for resolution extrapolation in DiTs.

DYPE is simple, training-free, and introduces no inference overhead, making it highly practical; the unifying observation that PI/NTK-aware/YaRN all collapse to the identity when s=1 leads naturally to the time-parameterized scheduler κ(t).

The evaluation is broad: text-to-image on FLUX across four resolutions and two aspect ratios on two benchmarks (Tab. 1), class-conditional ImageNet generation on FiTv2 with three base extrapolation methods (Tab. 3), a human study (Tab. 2), a resolution-scaling analysis up to 6144² (Fig. 5), panorama generation (Tab. 8), a comparison against FreeScale (Tab. 7), and an ablation of scheduler designs (Tabs. 5-6).

The gains are largest precisely where the hypothesis predicts—at the highest resolutions (e.g., 4096²: CLIP 26.94 vs. 25.71 for YaRN vs. 16.43 for FLUX), and the comparison with Lumina-Next's time-aware RoPE (Tab. 4) directly tests the central design decision against the closest prior idea.
Appendix D ablations provide useful design guidance (multiplicative vs. exponential scheduling, applying κ(t) to NTK vs. by-parts components), supporting the method's internal coherence.
weaknesses: The core method is a fairly small modification of existing extrapolation schemes (injecting a two-hyperparameter schedule κ(t) = λs·t^λt into PI/NTK/YaRN), and the choice of this specific power-law form appears empirical rather than derived from the spectral analysis in Sec. 3.1; the connection between the progression map γ(f,t) and the particular schedule is loose.

Statistical robustness of the quantitative results is a concern: FID on Aesthetic-4K is computed over only 195 image–prompt pairs, so differences of a few points (e.g., 186.00 vs. 192.19 vs. 195.68) are within plausible noise; no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed runs are reported for any benchmark.

Some ablation results are internally inconsistent with the paper's narrative: DY-NTK at 320² has worse sFID (14.29) than vanilla NTK (14.35, essentially tied) and DY-YaRN's sFID at 384² (33.92) is worse than YaRN's (36.09 is worse, but the trend flips between FiTv2 baseline 49.51 and all extrapolation methods), and FLUX's baseline ImageReward is strongly negative at some resolutions (-0.28, -0.53), suggesting weak baselines at those settings; the portrait/landscape asymmetry (gap widening with DYPE) is noted but not explained.

The human study is limited to 20 prompts and only compares DYPE variants against their static counterparts; ~88-90% preference rates are large, but the small prompt set and lack of comparison against FLUX itself limit interpretability.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the project page link is blank in the manuscript, no code release is stated, and there is a broken/placeholder reference ('Placeholder YourTeam, arXiv:2025.xxxxx') plus a malformed citation (Betker et al.) that undermine polish; the FiTv2 result in Tab. 3 also cites Wang et al. (2024) while the intro cites 'YourTeam (2025)' for what appears to be the same work, which is confusing.

There is no explicit limitations section; aspects such as dependence on hyperparameters λs/λt per resolution, the method's behavior on non-FLUX DiT architectures beyond FiTv2, and the assumption that image RoPE frequencies align with image Fourier frequencies (RoPE dimension index vs. spatial frequency is only loosely connected) are not discussed.

The spectral analysis (Eq. 10-11, Fig. 2a) is performed with a denoiser trained on ImageNet and relies on an idealized mixture model with an assumed 1/f^ω spectrum (ω≈2); it does not directly characterize the FLUX latent-space process on which the method is applied, so the theory–experiment link is indirect.

Metrics like CLIPScore and ImageReward are computed on ultra-high-resolution images although these evaluators were trained on low-resolution data; the evaluation protocol for resizing/downsampling is described only for Aesthetic-4K, and the very high absolute FID values (180-260) suggest a nonstandard protocol that should be clarified.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: exploiting the empirically demonstrated spectral progression of diffusion sampling (low frequencies converge early, high frequencies evolve throughout; Fig. 2, Eq. 11-12) to make position extrapolation (PI/NTK/YaRN) timestep-aware. The resulting method is simple, training-free, and adds no sampling overhead.

The method is directly and carefully positioned against the most closely related work (Lumina-Next's Time-Aware Scaled RoPE / TASR), with a clear argument for why the opposite scheduling direction (shifting toward no-scaling/extrapolation late in sampling) is preferable, supported by both quantitative (Tab. 5) and qualitative (Fig. 8) comparisons.

Unusually broad empirical validation for this line of work: FLUX at 2048x3072 through 4096x4096 across DrawBench and Aesthetic-4K (Tab. 1), comparison against many non-PE baselines including fine-tuning-based and U-Net-based methods (Tab. 3), class-conditional ImageNet generation with FiTv2 (Tab. 4), Qwen-Image (Tab. 8), video generation with Wan2.1 via VBench (Tab. 9), image editing, and panoramic generation. Human evaluation (50 raters, Tab. 2) and a resolution-scaling analysis (Fig. 5) further support the claims.
Gains are consistent and grow with resolution, which matches the paper's central claim; the attention-entropy analysis (Appendix F) provides a plausible mechanistic account of why the method works.

Ablations in Appendix D on scheduler family (multiplicative vs. exponential), lambda_s and lambda_t values, and where to apply the scheduler within YaRN (NTK term vs. by-parts ramp) show the design choices were not arbitrary and that the low-to-high frequency idea drives the improvement.
Writing and presentation are generally clear, with a useful unifying notation for PI/NTK/YaRN (Sec. 2.2) that makes the method easy to follow.
weaknesses: The theoretical link between PSD evolution (Eq. 11-12) and the required PE frequency allocation is heuristic. The paper observes low-frequency convergence, then assumes that 'evolving modes depend more on their corresponding frequency representation in the PE than the converged ones' — this causal assumption is stated but not directly validated; the analysis motivates rather than derives the specific kappa(t) = lambda_s * t^lambda_t form, which is ultimately a two-parameter heuristic tuned by ablation.

The core novelty is modest: it is a time-dependent modulation of existing extrapolation schemes (PI/NTK/YaRN), and time-aware PE schedules for diffusion already exist (Lumina-Next/TASR); the contribution is primarily the opposite scheduling direction plus its empirical justification rather than a new mechanism.

Metric reliability is a concern: CLIPScore, ImageReward, and Aesthetics scores are known to be unreliable for ultra-high-resolution images (they are computed on downsampled or differently-processed images), and the FID values (140-220) suggest the reference protocol differs substantially from standard settings, making absolute numbers hard to interpret and cross-paper comparisons delicate. No seed/variance reporting for any quantitative table.

Some quantitative gains are small and within plausible metric noise for the better variants (e.g., DY-NTK vs. NTK on Aesthetic-4K FID, DY-YaRN vs. YaRN at moderate resolutions), so the strength of the evidence varies across resolutions and metrics; the most convincing results are the extreme-resolution cases (3072^2, 4096^2).
Human evaluation uses only 20 prompts (a subset of Aesthetic-4K), limiting its statistical power.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code is promised 'upon acceptance,' and several details (e.g., exact downsampling protocol for FID/CLIP, latent-space vs. pixel-space choices) are deferred; hyperparameters are fixed to lambda_s = lambda_t = 2 for FLUX with limited discussion of how they should be set for a new model/resolution.
No dedicated limitations section; degradation beyond 6144^2 and aspect-ratio bias are mentioned in passing but not systematically discussed.

strengths: The paper is grounded in a clear, well-motivated observation: a Fourier-space analysis (Eq. 11-12, Fig. 2) showing that low-frequency components of the mixture distribution qt converge early while high-frequency modes evolve throughout sampling. This gives the method a principled (if heuristic) rationale rather than being a purely empirical tweak.

The proposed modification is simple, training-free, and adds no inference overhead, which makes it broadly applicable. The unifying observation that PI, NTK-aware, and YaRN all collapse to no scaling when s=1 is elegant and leads naturally to the time-parameterized family κ(t)=λs·t^λt.

Evaluation breadth is strong: FLUX (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K), FiTv2 on ImageNet class-conditional generation, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1 video generation, image editing, and panoramic generation, with comparisons against both PE-based baselines (PI, NTK, YaRN, TASR) and general high-resolution pipelines (HiFlow, UltraPixel, Diffusion-4K, DemoFusion, etc.).

Consistent improvements over the strongest static baseline (YaRN), with gains growing at higher resolutions (e.g., 4096^2 in Tab. 1), and a resolution-scaling analysis (Fig. 5) showing the method extends the usable resolution range.

Useful ablations (scheduler form, λs/λt, where κ(t) is applied in YaRN; Tabs. 6-7) and a supporting attention-entropy analysis (Appendix F) that connects the method to a known failure mode of resolution extrapolation.

Honest related-work positioning: the paper clearly distinguishes its conclusions from Lumina-Next/TASR (Zhuo et al., 2024), which uses time-aware scaling in the opposite direction, and includes a direct comparison (Tab. 5).
weaknesses: The central design assumption — that modes still evolving during sampling depend more strongly on their corresponding PE frequencies, and that operating the denoiser at its trained PE conditions is beneficial late in sampling — is stated but never directly validated. The chain from the spectral progression map (Fig. 2b) to the specific functional form κ(t)=λs·t^λt is loose; the analysis motivates 'time-dependent scaling' generically rather than this particular scheduler.

The scheduler is heavily hand-tuned (λs=λt=2 fixed globally, α=1, β=32) and it is unclear whether these constants transfer across resolutions, models, and sampling step counts. The ablations are conducted only at 3072^2 on a 50-prompt DrawBench subset, so the generality of the hyperparameters is not established.

Some reported gains over the static baselines are modest and within plausible noise, yet no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance are reported anywhere (e.g., CLIPScore differences of ~0.1-0.2 in Tab. 1; DY-NTK vs. NTK at 3072x2048 differs by only 0.04 FID).

Absolute FID values (~180-200) on Aesthetic-4K are unusually high and the evaluation protocol (downsampling 4K reference images to match target resolutions, patch-FID on ~195 curated pairs) is non-standard; the validity and comparability of these FID/patch-FID numbers across methods deserve more scrutiny and discussion.

Human evaluation (Tab. 2) covers only 20 prompts, 50 raters, pairwise comparisons between DYPE variants and their static parents; no inter-rater agreement, no comparison against the strongest non-PE baselines (e.g., HiFlow), and unclear blinding/protocol details.

The method requires choosing among three variants (DY-PI, DY-NTK, DY-YaRN) plus scheduler hyperparameters per backbone; there is no guidance or unified recipe, and in some settings DY-PI remains far below the base model (Tab. 4), suggesting the approach is not uniformly reliable.
The derivation is restricted to the linear flow-matching schedule; applicability to other schedules (VP, DDPM-style) is asserted but not analyzed or tested.

Presentation issues: several tables (Tab. 1, Tab. 4) are dense and hard to parse; occasional typos ('extensioN', 'the the trade-off exiting extrapolation method'); the claim of 'no additional sampling cost' should be qualified since evaluation requires many runs and the memory footprint at 16M+ pixels is not reported.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: the paper derives the time-dependent power spectral density of the flow-matching trajectory (Eq. 11) and uses it to justify a time-parameterized scaling κ(t) = λs·t^λt applied to existing extrapolation schemes (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN). The insight that low-frequency modes converge early while high frequencies evolve throughout sampling is intuitively appealing and well illustrated in Fig. 2.

Extensive empirical evaluation: results span multiple architectures (FLUX, FiTv2-XL/2, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1 video), multiple benchmarks (DrawBench, Aesthetic-4K, ImageNet, VBench), multiple resolutions and aspect ratios, plus application domains (editing, panorama). Resolution-scaling analysis (Fig. 5) convincingly shows the method extends the usable resolution range beyond static YaRN.

Thorough comparison with both PE-based baselines (NTK, YaRN, TASR) and general tuning-free high-resolution pipelines (HiFlow, UltraPixel, DemoFusion, etc.), with reasonable protocols for patch-based metrics and downsampled FID.

Ablation studies (Appendix D) on scheduler family, magnitudes, and where the timestep dependence is applied in YaRN, plus a human preference study and an attention-entropy analysis (Appendix F) that provides a mechanistic account of why the method works.
Training-free with no inference overhead, and consistent gains that grow with resolution, which is a practically useful property.
Honest positioning against closely related prior work (Lumina-Next's time-aware scaled RoPE), including direct empirical comparison in Appendix B and Tab. 5.
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: the core contribution is making the scaling factor of existing PI/NTK/YaRN schemes timestep-dependent via a two-parameter power-law schedule. This is a relatively simple modification, closely adjacent to Lumina-Next's time-aware scaling; the difference (moving toward no-scaling vs. PI-to-NTK interpolation) is argued but not derived.

The theoretical analysis is partly heuristic: the derivation in Sec. 3.1 assumes the idealized linear flow-matching mixture with independent Gaussian noise and a known power-law data spectrum; the leap from the observed spectral progression to the specific schedule κ(t) = λs·t^λt with λs = λt = 2 is not principled — the hyperparameters appear tuned rather than predicted by the analysis, and the ablation covers only 50 prompts at a single resolution.

Mixed results for one variant at extreme resolutions: at 4096×4096, DY-NTK degrades substantially on text alignment (CLIP 21.51 vs. YaRN 25.71), and it is really only DY-YaRN that is consistently strong. The paper does not clearly explain when/why the dynamic scheme can hurt, weakening the generality claim.

Metric reliability concerns: FID values are very high (~180-200), suggesting non-standard reference sets/protocols for downsampling; CLIPScore differences are often small (<0.5); the human study covers only 20 prompts. Some claims of 'state-of-the-art fidelity' rest on these noisy measurements, and on 4096² Aesthetic-4K the FID ordering does not uniformly favor the method.

Reproducibility is limited: code is only promised 'upon acceptance'; implementation details in Appendix C are brief (α, β, λ values, 28 steps) and omit important details such as how t maps to sampling steps, per-axis handling, and sampler choice; the potential sensitivity to these choices is not examined.

The spectral analysis is conducted on an ImageNet-trained denoiser but the headline results use FLUX; no verification that the assumed spectral ordering holds for the actual models being extrapolated at 4K.
Some typos and rough edges (e.g., broken 'Project page' link, duplicated references, garbled appendix text) that slightly detract from presentation.
